problem:
Express $z=\sqrt{3}-\text{i}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give the **exact** values of $r$ and $\theta ,$ in **radians** from $[0,2\pi ).$

$z=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(${{field-2}}$)+\,i\operatorname{sin}⁡(${{field-3}}$))$
worked_solution:
In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\sqrt{3}-\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta $ represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\sqrt{3}>0$ and $y=-1<0,$ $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}| \\  & =2\pi -arctan\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{11\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z=\sqrt{3}-\text{i}$ in polar form:

$$
z=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{6})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{6}))
$$
